newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentina eyes trade, investment in Chirac's visit.
newsitem.headline: Argentina eyes trade, investment in Chirac's visit.

text.p: Argentina sees French President Jacques Chirac's visit as a prime chance to attract more foreign investment, consolidate its regional trade bloc and improve its bargaining position with the United States.

In particular, it hopes Chirac's proposal to cement ties between the European Union and the Mercosur trade bloc formed by Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay and Uruguay will give the group more leverage in future free trade talks with Washington.
"It improves Mercosur's negotiating stance," said a government official who asked not to be identified.

The French leader, accompanied by 20 leading businessmen seeking trade and investment opportunities, will arrive on Sunday in Buenos Aires as part of a Latin American tour also including Brazil, Uruguay and Bolivia.
In Brazil on Wednesday, he proposed holding a EU-Mercosur summit followed by an EU-Latin American summit next year.
"Mercosur is growing diplomatically, it's becoming an important meeting point," the Argentine official said.

The group, which launched a customs union in 1995, quickly exceeded its initial goals, tightening commercial and political ties. It has also expanded, clinching free trade deals with Chile and Bolivia last year. Other regional nations have also expressed interest in similar pacts.

Washington's proposal to set up a pan-American free-trade zone -- launched by former President George Bush and later embraced by President Bill Clinton, who will be touring Latin America in May -- met a warm welcome throughout the region.

The area, which after decades of military regimes and trade protectionism has finally embarked on a free market and democratic path, welcomed the idea as a golden opportunity to boost growth and consolidate civilian rule.

But Brazil and Argentina slowly came to the conclusion that Mercosur was too valuable a tool to let it dissolve into a pan-American free trade area whose terms they fear would be dictated by the powerful NAFTA -- the free trade zone comprising the United States, Canada and Mexico.

Brazil vocally and Argentina more timidly now say that while they still want free trade with Washington they would like to see Mercosur consolidate and grow first, so it can improve its bargaining position before facing the world's dominant power at the negotiating table.

Tariff-free access to Europe -- hoped for by 2005 -- and Chirac's new impetus in promoting Euro-Latin ties would, on top of the obvious trade and investment benefits, fortify Mercosur's leverage, they say.
The French leader has been clear about his intentions.

"Latin America's future is not on the North-South axis, but with Europe," he said before departing from Paris. "Its essential economic interests -- trade, investment, aid -- lie not with the United States but with Europe."

France is also a key investor in Argentina, with more than $4 billion in direct investment since President Carlos Menem threw open the economy and launched a major privatisation drive after starting his first term in office in 1989.

Electricite de France, France Cable et Radio, Lyonnaise des Eaux and Generale des Aux got a big chunk of Argentina's utilities when they were sold. Other major French players include food group Danone, supermaket chain Carrefour and carmakers Peugeot and Renault.
Argentina's two-way trade with the EU has grown steadily, reaching $11.5 billion last year, far exceeding the $7.9 billion traded with NAFTA.
